title: Swift Foot
type: Harengon ranger · scout and contested martyr
dek: A scout and advocate for ordinary lives whose wit, compassion and opposition to imposed servitude lead toward a final demonstration with consequences he cannot control.

facts.Legacy: Swift the Martyr · contested among Rahu and companions

body:
Swift Foot was a Harengon ranger, archer, scout, and explorer connected to Pristinia and its adventuring company. Grey fur and forest-green antlers made him recognizable; quick jokes, practical courage, and concern for ordinary people shaped how his companions remembered him.

Justice for people without adventurers’ power

At Pristinia’s civic debate on 13, Month of Physisia, Year 1, Swift wants the adventurers heard without letting them take over the people’s government. He asks why they are making decisions: to help the town, or to benefit themselves? A representative can speak for adventurers while the elders remain responsible to the people who live there.

He objects to offices whose terms effectively favor the longest-lived peoples, and worries about decisions made while an adventurer is away. He can accept a government he would not personally design if it gives his companions a respected voice. The town needs a system that works after powerful visitors leave.

You got to consider their lives, too. The regular person doesn’t have our resources.Swift Foot

He challenges execution because it prevents recompense and because a mistaken conviction cannot be repaired. He still accepts proportionate punishment, expulsion for extreme violence and the elders’ authority to investigate. His proposed protections against fraudulent goods distinguish a useless cosmetic from a false medicine on which a child’s life depends.

Even this serious argument has rabbit jokes, carrot juice and frustration when he feels unheard. Humor does not erase the precise institutional question: who carries the risk when adventurers use their own exceptional resources as the standard for everyone?

The scout who keeps joking

On 8, Month of Rebirth, Swift follows a distress signal underground with Lucido, Olokun, Dafty and the others. He offers to lead, carries an aid to navigation and volunteers to be lowered on a rope when someone has to take the risk. His courage includes needing to be pulled back up.

He jokes through poisoned coughing and a bad choice of passage, then defers to Lucido rather than insisting that leading once gives him every decision. When companions are hurt, he calls for support. The company reaches Scribonia and escapes into the sun, where Swift collapses and still asks whose call actually drew them in.

Am I still poisoned or did Luci just rhyme?Swift Foot, 8, Month of Rebirth, Year 1

Ada later calls him the new arrow on Pristinia’s horizon. Her remembrance catches a visible wit, but the quest also preserves exhaustion, uncertainty and concern for people he cannot keep safe alone.

Freedom, tea and the fatal demonstration

By 6, Month of Moirah, Year 1, Swift returns with a mission of his own. He cannot obtain the public support he wants and promises to make clear that he acts independently of Pristinia. He slips into the embassy grounds to speak to the workers.

Most move away. Ummo, the gardener, will listen quietly. Swift argues that a station assigned at birth need not decide a life and describes escaping a situation in which another person’s command had been made to seem normal. The full history behind that account remains unresolved.

Ummo says he likes his garden and home, yet admits wanting tea he is not allowed to have. Swift goes to fetch some without magic, hoping to demonstrate that someone denied magical power can still act. Unable to distinguish the teas, he brings the assortment back. Ummo calls him master and speaks of debt; Swift insists that he is no master.

The conversation does not become simple agreement. Ummo describes a social balance between labor and protection, while Swift grows frustrated and tries to expose what happens if the protectors cannot protect. He finds Strange Talon, strikes him from concealment and intends to wound him as a demonstration. Rahu witnesses later describe an assassination attempt. Intention, action and interpretation remain distinct.

Swift throws down his sword, claims sole responsibility and says Melian and Pristinia had no part in it. He deliberately stops defending himself, hoping Talon’s response will expose the system before its workers. Talon kills him. The narrator names him Swift the Martyr and confirms that the watching people will remember and talk.

The choice leaves a hard question beside the earlier advocate of recompense: he rejects domination, yet tries to change other people’s lives through a violent demonstration he cannot control. His death is real; neither his certainty nor the honor later paid to it completes anyone else’s freedom.

A contested martyr

The narration names him Swift the Martyr. Later accounts report Dasa talking about his actions, Ummo breaking free, and the chant “Swift Foot lives.” Rahu authorities continue condemning him as an attacker, while friends debate investigation, revenge, and how to honor him.

His legacy preserves both the advocate for ordinary lives and the danger of his final certainty. His death does not erase his wit or earlier service, and the later chant is testimony about remembrance rather than dialogue spoken by Swift himself.

Read Swift Foot’s lines in the quote gallery, grouped by freedom, justice, humor, and his final words.

10 October · remembrance becomes a request

Fresh graffiti honoring Swift draws another party toward the Rahu embassy. In its gardens, Dasa Kimi and Kuri ask for help obtaining freedom. Kimi says Swift lives in them and names Vey and Vaa as siblings inspired by his cause.

Di’trillio promises to find them. The scene supplies a new consequence of Swift’s death, not evidence that he has resurrected or that the Dasa have already won freedom. Read the Dasa’s appeal.

Scene sources: 1, 2, 3, 4.

Grief and the limits of vengeance

During the Swift Foot investigation, Dorian threatens three Rahu witnesses who repeat the account given by their captain. Vaemyr steps between them and refuses to let questioning become torture. Dorian withdraws; the witnesses maintain that they speak what they saw. Their agreement is testimony, not an independent resolution of Swift’s death. Vaemyr’s intervention shows what protecting a friend can require when grief turns toward violence.

Scene evidence: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.

The appeal reaches a refuge

The later northern expedition finds Vey and Vaa among a small Dasa refuge. Di’Trillio corrects his assumption that the siblings already lead an uprising: they offer another way to live, while some Dasa choose resistance and others seek passage away. He pledges practical support and accepts a sending stone.

The development gives Swift Foot’s remembered example a new consequence without reporting his bodily return or a completed liberation. Follow the expedition’s outcome →

Scene references: 1, 2, 3, 4.

A promise beside a wounded tree

The later quarry expedition draws out a less playful part of the same scout. Swift wants the workers to know whether the shaft is safe, checks passages and keeps watch. Puns continue while the danger becomes real.

After the fighting, wounded and blood-matted, he comforts a tree in Sylvan. He tells it that it held as long as it could, blames the company for arriving late and promises not to let the same thing happen to another. Those words are his response to a loss, not proof that he can control the next danger.

He then asks where the scouts were and leaves limping, heartsick and in need of rest. Thoughts turn toward Nimbus and a small realm in the Feywild before he pushes them away. The record establishes distress and a pull toward an earlier life; it does not fully recover that relationship or make his private need for comfort a failure of independence.

The first embassy visit hardens his opposition

At the Rahu embassy, Swift is uneasy before he can put every objection into words. An owl alarms him; execution, deference and the treatment of workers trouble him more. He asks what help costs and whether the workers genuinely choose the lives they are told to lead.

He remembers Nimbus while watching masks, authority and an exchange of valuable knowledge. The memories explain part of his reaction without proving that every Rahu person shares the motives he suspects.

Outside, he says he believes the Rahu want power over Pristinia and calls for the embassy to be driven out and burned. The intensity has moved beyond his earlier preference for hearing local people. His criticism of dependency remains important, but it does not make every action he proposes safe or representative of the town.

nodes.history: Swift attacks Talon from concealment, then claims responsibility and refuses to continue fighting. Rahu witnesses describe an assassination attempt; the dossier records Swift’s intention to demonstrate coercive power.
nodes.consequence: His intent, his attack, and the witnesses’ interpretation remain distinct.
nodes.evidence: Swift Foot dossier and Strange Talon biography; no interpretation erases the attack.

moments.text: Swift wounds Talon, separates his act from Pristinia and Melian, and deliberately stops fighting.
Talon kills him; later accounts contest what his final stand meant.

nodes.relation: The official account his friends question
nodes.history: Hildethrax recounts the Rahu account of Swift’s attack. Vaemyr searches that account for deception while grieving his friend.
nodes.consequence: The testimony shapes the contested legacy without becoming omniscient narration.
nodes.evidence: Swift Foot and Dale/Vaemyr dossiers; an attributed witness account, not evidence that Hildethrax and Swift shared a personal bond.

moments.text: Hildethrax describes the attack and its aftermath to the investigators.

nodes.subtitle: A friend protects the standard of truth
nodes.relation: A friend protects the standard of truth
nodes.history: Vaemyr grieves Swift and wants the Rahu account to be wrong. He stops Dorian from torturing witnesses, then continues questioning them.
nodes.consequence: Remembrance becomes careful investigation rather than permission to force a preferred answer.
nodes.evidence: Dale/Vaemyr dossier; exact dates within the later exchanges remain incomplete.

moments.text: Vaemyr seeks evidence about his friend’s death.
He intervenes against torture while refusing to abandon the investigation.
